linkedin_activity.text: I've been talking about "Scientific Loyalty" for quite some time. Today, I came across Veeva's latest Agentic Commercial Trends Report, and it feels like another strong signal that our industry is moving in exactly this direction. One statistic immediately stood out: ➡️ 65% of AI-generated call reports contained actionable treatment barriers that traditional CRM reports completely missed. Think about that for a moment. For years we've optimized structured CRM data: Call frequency Segmentation Reach Channels Activities But the real value often lives between the fields. Why is a physician hesitant? Why is a treatment not adopted? Why is reimbursement creating friction? Why is the office staff frustrated? Those conversations rarely fit into a dropdown menu. Agentic AI is beginning to transform those qualitative conversations into what Veeva calls Commercial Evidence. Actionable intelligence extracted from natural interactions. The report also shows impressive commercial outcomes: • 7× increase in high-value actions from compliant conversational AI • 38% more requests for HCP conversations • Continuous visibility into the real questions physicians and patients are asking online, allowing companies to improve content and customer journeys in near real time. This is where I believe the conversation becomes even more interesting. For me, the destination isn't simply better commercial evidence. It's Scientific Loyalty. Because loyalty in healthcare has never been about points, discounts or marketing campaigns. It is built when a company consistently helps healthcare professionals solve real scientific and clinical problems. Imagine combining: ✔️ Agentic call reports ✔️ Conversational AI ✔️ Medical insights ✔️ Congress interactions ✔️ Real-world evidence ✔️ Patient support experiences ...into one continuously learning system. Not just to predict the next best action. But to understand the next best scientific conversation. That's a fundamentally different model of engagement. One that moves pharma from tracking interactions to earning trust. I believe that's where AI creates its biggest competitive advantage. Not replacing people, but helping organizations understand humans better than ever before. ...more

One of the most interesting pharma AI reports I’ve read recently. A lot of discussions around AI in pharma still focus on tools, copilots and experimentation. But this report from ZS and Mahmood Majeed points to something much bigger: 💡 The real transformation is shifting from technology experimentation toward operating model redesign. A few findings that stood out to me: → Leaders are moving from “Where can AI work?” to “Where will AI drive measurable growth?” → Only ~40% of AI pilots make it to scaled deployment → 68% say poor data quality and governance are among the top reasons AI initiatives fail → Domain expertise and process understanding are becoming critical for AI success → AI agents are increasingly tied to workflow orchestration and decision support That last point is especially important. For years, pharma engagement systems were primarily designed as: 🔴 systems of record 🔴 activity tracking platforms 🔴 channel orchestration tools But AI is changing the expectation. The next generation of engagement platforms will likely evolve into: 🟢 systems of guidance 🟢 systems of prioritization 🟢 adaptive engagement engines 🟢 scientific decision support layers This is also one of the reasons why I’ve been thinking more and more about Scientific Loyalty not simply as a framework, but as a potential operating model for scientific engagement. Because the challenge is no longer: “How do we collect more interaction data?” The challenge is: “How do we create context-rich, scientifically valuable engagement at scale while helping teams make better decisions in increasingly complex ecosystems?” That requires much more than AI alone. It requires: 1️⃣ stronger operating models 2️⃣ clearer governance 3️⃣ better workflow design 4️⃣ longitudinal relationship intelligence 5️⃣ domain context 6️⃣ human + AI collaboration Feels like pharma is slowly moving in that direction. ...more

Governance Is Where Loyalty Is Won or Lost In digital transformation, governance is often seen as a control mechanism. Approvals. Processes. Standards. Alignment loops. Necessary — but rarely loved. But the more I think about Scientific Loyalty, the clearer it becomes: Governance is not just about control. It’s about protecting the experience at scale. Because without it, things drift. one team optimizes for speed another for compliance another for local needs another for global consistency Individually, all decisions make sense. Collectively, they create fragmentation. And fragmentation is where loyalty breaks. Scientific Loyalty requires a different approach to governance. Not heavier. Not slower. But more intentional. Governance should answer questions like: Does this reduce or increase effort for the user? Does this create clarity or add complexity? Does this strengthen trust — or weaken it over time? Does this decision hold across the full journey, not just one touchpoint? If governance doesn’t ask these questions, it becomes operational. If it does, it becomes strategic. Because at scale, loyalty isn’t shaped by single features. It’s shaped by the decisions that governance allows — and prevents. ...more

Most loyalty programs reward transactions. The good ones reward behavior. The best ones reward values. I came across a simple but powerful example from Accor’s ALL – Accor Live Limitless: → Choose a plant-forward meal → Scan a QR code → Get rewarded with loyalty points That’s it. But look closer at what’s really happening: This isn’t just a perk. It’s a signal. A signal that says: “We value sustainability, conscious choices, and your wellbeing.” And suddenly, loyalty shifts from: 👉 “Stay more, earn more” to 👉 “Act in line with what matters, and we’ll recognize it” That’s a completely different relationship. It builds: • Trust (shared values) • Emotional connection (feels meaningful, not transactional) • Long-term behavior change (not just one-off rewards) Now here’s the interesting question: 👉 What would this look like in pharma? Instead of rewarding activity… What if we rewarded scientific engagement that actually improves outcomes? Imagine: • HCPs recognized for continuous learning on new evidence • Engagement points for applying guidelines in practice • Value signals tied to patient impact—not just interactions This is where Scientific Loyalty starts to become real. Not points for clicks. But recognition for better decisions. And that’s how you move from CRM… to trust infrastructure. ...more

Pharma CRM is starting to look a lot like the music industry. That’s not a compliment. When recording technology disrupted music, everyone rushed to “fix” it: – New rules – New intermediaries – New systems to control value The result? More complexity. More bureaucracy. And often… less value reaching the actual creators. Sound familiar? Right now in pharma: – We’re layering CRM, marketing automation, data platforms, AI – We’re adding governance, processes, approvals – We’re trying to “control” engagement But here’s the uncomfortable truth: Complexity doesn’t create value. It hides where value is lost. Most systems today don’t fail because of missing features. They fail because: – incentives are misaligned – ownership is unclear – value doesn’t flow to the right place And AI will amplify this. Fast. So instead of asking: “How do we build more systems?” Maybe the better question is: “How does value actually flow through this system and where does it break?” That’s the lens we’re starting to apply with Scientific Loyalty. Less control. More clarity. Less bureaucracy. More value. Curious how others are seeing this shift 👇 ...more

Sweden just did something unexpected. After years of pushing digital learning in schools, they’re going back to… books, paper, and pens. Yes, really. And the reason is uncomfortable 👇 📉 Literacy levels dropped 📉 Focus decreased 📉 Students struggled more with comprehension Too much screen time. Too little actual learning. So now they’re reversing course. At first glance, this sounds like a step backwards. But it’s not. It’s a correction. Because the real problem was never “digital vs. analog”. It was this: 👉 Technology was introduced without a clear purpose. Devices became the solution Instead of serving the outcome If you work in product, this should feel VERY familiar. How often do we: - Roll out new tools without clear user value? - Add features instead of improving outcomes? - Confuse “more digital” with “better experience”? Sweden didn’t fail because of tech. They failed because of how they used it. And now they’re overcorrecting. From “everything digital” → to “almost no screens” But the truth is somewhere in the middle. The winning approach is simple: 👉 Design the experience first 👉 Then choose the right tools (digital OR analog) There’s a lesson here beyond education. Especially in pharma, CRM, and customer engagement. Right now, many organizations are doing exactly what Sweden did: - More tools - More channels - More automation But not more impact. That’s where most strategies fall apart. Because: ❌ More digital ≠ more meaningful ❌ More touchpoints ≠ better relationships The real opportunity? 👉 Move from “digital engagement” to meaningful interaction design That’s where real loyalty is built. Not through tools. Through relevance, timing, and human understanding. Sweden’s shift isn’t anti-tech. It’s a reminder: If you don’t design for outcomes… Even the best technology will fail. Curious to hear your take: Are we overusing digital tools in our products today? Or are we still not using them well enough? ...more

Most companies think they understand loyalty. They don’t. They measure retention. They track tenure. They celebrate low attrition. But staying ≠ loyalty. People stay for very different reasons: – Belief – Comfort – Fear – Money Only one of them is real loyalty. The rest is just disguised retention. Here’s the uncomfortable truth: Loyalty is hard to measure. But disloyalty isn’t. You can see it everywhere: – Less initiative – No ownership – Cynicism in conversations – “Just doing the job” mindset – Quiet LinkedIn updates – Taking recruiter calls These are not random signals. They are leading indicators of disloyalty. And yet, most organizations don’t track them. They wait until people leave… and call it “unexpected attrition.” It’s not unexpected. It was invisible. This is where I believe we need a shift: Instead of asking “Are our employees loyal?” We should ask “How close are they to leaving — mentally or physically?” Because loyalty doesn’t disappear overnight. It erodes. Slowly. Quietly. Predictably. And the same applies beyond employees. In pharma, in CRM, in any relationship system: We don’t lose people suddenly. We lose them long before we notice. Maybe the real problem isn’t loyalty. It’s our inability to detect disloyalty early enough. ...more

Not Everything Needs to Go According to Plan Wednesday felt like early spring. Sun. Warmth. Almost 15 degrees. Yesterday I woke up to this. A completely different landscape. Snow covering everything. Silence. Stillness. A reset. It would be easy to see this as a disruption. Plans change. Expectations shift. The “flow” gets interrupted. But standing there that morning, I realized something: Not every surprise is a problem to solve. Some are just a different experience to accept. In product work and in life we spend a lot of time trying to control outcomes. Roadmaps. Timelines. Forecasts. Plans. And then reality happens. Things change. Context shifts. New constraints appear. The instinct is often to resist. But sometimes the better move is simpler: accept, adapt, and see what this new situation makes possible. Because not everything that breaks the plan breaks the progress. Some things just change the perspective. ...more

Thanks, Maciej! Really appreciate your thoughtful perspective. You're absolutely right. Today I don't think Scientific Value is measured consistently yet. Most organizations still optimize for activity and operational efficiency, while the scientific impact of an interaction remains largely implicit. The way I currently think about it is that Scientific Value isn't a single KPI, but a combination of dimensions such as: • Scientific relevance (was the discussion aligned with the HCP's needs?) • Depth of scientific exchange • Evidence quality and credibility • Knowledge progression over time • Long-term impact on scientific engagement None of these are perfect on their own, but together they could provide a much richer picture than traditional activity metrics. And I completely agree with your point on governance - without MLR and the right guardrails around conversational AI, scaling this responsibly won't happen. That's probably one of the biggest enablers (and bottlenecks) over the next few years.

Redcare Pharmacy accelerates in Q2: 20% revenue growth, expanding EBITDA margin; International turning profitable. Our Q2 2026 results were published today and they reflect the dedication and collaboration of our teams across all markets. Together, we continue to drive sustainable growth, strengthen profitability and deliver an outstanding experience for our customers. Q2 highlights: • Group revenue increased 20% year over year to EUR 853 million. • Group non-Rx revenue grew 13%, while Rx revenue increased 34%. • Rx Germany continued its strong momentum with 58% growth. • The active customer base increased by 0.5 million during Q2 to 14.7 million. • Adjusted EBITDA increased 63% to EUR 29.6 million; the margin improved to 3.5%. • Upgraded full-year 2026 guidance confirmed. As our CEO Olaf Heinrich said: "Q2 was another strong quarter for Redcare Pharmacy. Growth accelerated, Rx Germany continued its strong momentum and profitability improved significantly. We also welcomed another half million active customers, bringing our active customer base to 14.7 million. Most notably, our International segment delivered positive EBITDA for the first time – an important milestone that reflects the progress we have made in scaling the business sustainably." A sincere thank you to all colleagues whose commitment and expertise made these results possible. Your focus on our customers and your daily efforts continue to move Redcare Pharmacy forward.

🛒 𝐀𝐋𝐃𝐈 𝐒ü𝐝 𝐬𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐚 𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐛𝐮𝐢𝐥𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐚 𝐥𝐨𝐲𝐚𝐥𝐭𝐲 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐠𝐫𝐚𝐦. 𝐓𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐦𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐡 𝐢𝐭 𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐚𝐝𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐭𝐢𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐢𝐭 𝐡𝐚𝐬𝐧'𝐭 𝐠𝐨𝐭 𝐨𝐧𝐞. A pattern I keep seeing. ✨ Both things are true. ALDI Süd tested loyalty features in its app in Scotland from last autumn, built around points, games and challenges rather than pure discounts. In July the trial was stopped. On 20 July the German campaign launched: "Günstig ohne Bonus-App. Keine Punkte. Keine Coupons. Kein Stress." (Low prices without a bonus app. No points. No coupons. No stress.) Proof point: price winner in the Kundenmonitor, sixteenth year running. 🔸 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐢𝐫 𝐜𝐫𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐜𝐢𝐬𝐦 𝐢𝐬 𝐟𝐚𝐢𝐫. ALDI calls app pricing a two-class checkout, where the person with the app pays less than the person without it. That is the sharpest description of discount-led loyalty I have heard from anyone, and it came from a competitor. 🔸 𝐁𝐮𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐮𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐢𝐬 𝐚𝐛𝐨𝐮𝐭 𝐝𝐢𝐬𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭𝐬, 𝐧𝐨𝐭 𝐥𝐨𝐲𝐚𝐥𝐭𝐲. Every grocer, ALDI included, needs to reach its customers individually: inspire them, guide them, stay useful along the journey. A leaflet cannot do that, and neither can a shelf price. 🔸 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐒𝐜𝐨𝐭𝐭𝐢𝐬𝐡 𝐝𝐞𝐬𝐢𝐠𝐧 𝐰𝐚𝐬 𝐚𝐢𝐦𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐚𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐫𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐠. Points, games, challenges. No price differentiation at the till. That is the hardest version of the problem, and stopping it says more about difficulty than about direction. 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐛𝐢𝐠𝐠𝐞𝐫 𝐩𝐢𝐜𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐞: Grocery loyalty has spent twenty years buying attention with margin. The next program that wins in this sector will earn attention with relevance instead: individual communication, inspiration, and a reason to open the app that has nothing to do with a coupon. Nobody has fully built that yet. Whoever does will make the two-class checkout obsolete without giving up the customer relationship. Can a grocery loyalty program work without a single discount? 💬 #Loyalty #CustomerEquity #Retail #Grocery

Twenty years ago I got a job because I spoke Portuguese. I hadn't learned it for my career — I'd learned it because a Brazilian martial art demanded it, because the songs meant something and I wanted to know what. That accident became a pattern I only understood much later: the skills that don't show up on a CV are often the ones that end up mattering most. I spent the next two decades running a capoeira school and managing corporate projects in parallel, and eventually started noticing how often they were teaching me the same lessons — about resilience, about teams, about change — just in different languages. I wrote them down. The book is called Never Fully Still, and it's out worldwide September 1. If you want to see how this plays out for your own team, I built a 2-minute diagnostic based on the book's framework — link in the comments.
